title.en: Anansi and Brother Dead: the Silent Host
title.zh: 蜘蛛人與死神兄弟：沉默的主人

region.zh: 牙買加雞窩地懷特霍爾

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 27a 'Brother Dead's Wife' (told by Grace Doran, Whitehall)

summary.en: In the wood Anansi finds a silent man drying meat on a barbecue and, receiving no answers to any question, helps himself to breakfast, pot, and meat — then leaves his daughter Sindy as 'servant' for the host. When the spider returns and finds only a ringed finger among the drying meat, he ties the silent Brother Dead's long hair to the trees, piles trash on the braids, and sets fire to them; the freed ghost looses his bow and arrow after him, and Anansi, standing on his house-top telling his children to jump down into Brother Dead's open hands, drops last into the dirt himself — which is why Anansi lives in the dirt.
summary.zh: 林中蜘蛛人遇沉默晾肉之人，問而不答，便自取早飯、鍋與肉，還留女兒辛迪作『僕』。再訪時乾肉間只見一截戴戒指的手指；蜘蛛人把死神兄弟的長髮縛上樹，堆碎柴於辮上點火。解縛的鬼魂張弓追射；蜘蛛人立在屋頂命孩子們一個個跳進死神張開的手中，自己最後一跳落進塵土——蜘蛛人從此住在塵土裡。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale with 'Brother Dead' (duppy) figure; told as entertainment at wake-nights, not restricted material.

passages.text: Anansi walked till he came into a wood where a man had a barbecue, plenty of meat drying. 'Hi, Brar! how you do?' — no answer. 'Brar, you have plenty meat and want someone to stay with you?' — no answer. 'Brar, give me a little breakfast?' — no answer. So Anansi went up on the barbecue, took the meat, asked for the pot, put it on, cooked, packed his bag, and said, 'Tomorrow I come back, and I see you need a servant, and I going to bring one of me daughter.' The daughter, Sindy, was left to cook for the silent host.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 27a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next visit, Brother Dead sat combing his long hair over his face, holding bow and arrow, and said not one word; Anansi went up on the barbecue and found his daughter's finger with a ring on it among the meat. 'I make you speak today!' He took the Dead man's hair, tied one long plait here, one there, two plaits behind to the trees; then piled dry trash and lit fire to the head. The plaits burned off, the Dead shook his head free, took up his bow and arrow and ran after Anansi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 27a, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Anansi ran up to his house: 'Wife and pickney, go up aloft, Brar Dead dah come!' Brother Dead came in and sat waiting, hands open. 'Pupa, me hungry!' cried the children. 'Brar Dead, open your hand, pickney a come!' — six children went into the open hands, one after another. Then Mrs. Anansi cried out, 'Brar Dead, open your hand, me a come!' — and Anansi dropped now, dropped in the dirt. From that time you see Anansi live in the dirt.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 27a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Brother Dead and the Brindle Puppy

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 28 'Brother Dead and the Brindle Puppy' (told by Charles Roe, Maroon Town)

summary.en: The old witch Brother Dead never speaks to anyone — to speak is to die — and spends his days shooting wild animals and drying them uneaten. Anansi robs his meat-bag twice; on the second visit he coaches the brindle puppy: when Brother Dead sings his hunting-song and people drop dead, throw green bush on them. The witch tracks Anansi by blood on his arrow-points, sings the old medicine-song — 'Anansi ma shway...' — catches him, skewers him through the ears, and burns him to dust.
summary.zh: 老巫死神兄弟從不與人言語——開口即死——終日射殺野獸晾乾而不食。蜘蛛人兩次竊肉；第二次他密授斑紋小狗：若死神唱歌令人倒斃，便將青草擲於屍上救活。死神以箭血循跡追蹤，唱起古咒之歌『Anansi ma shway……』，擒住蜘蛛人，以弓貫其雙耳，堆火焚為灰燼。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; 'Brother Dead' is a duppy/witch figure of wake-night entertainment. Song transcribed phonetically in source; paraphrase given.

passages.text: There was an old witch called Brar Dead, who never talked to anybody — if he talked to anybody, he would be dead. He only made bows all day and set them to catch all wild animals, and when he caught them he put them over the fire and dried them, but never ate them. Mr. Anansi went there one day, said, 'Brar Dead, give me some of your meat now,' got no answer for his pains, went in and took a whole bagful of the dried meat and started to eat it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 28 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Brother Dead had a brindle puppy. He picked some green bush and gave it to the puppy, and Anansi — meaning to make him talk that very day — told the little dog: when he sings and people drop dead, the puppy must throw the bush on them, to bring them back. The witch stuck his arrow-points in the ground at the crossroads, tracked the bleeding prints to Anansi's path, and sang his song — 'Anansi ma shway, Anansi ma shway; a pupa yan kin baw, eh, eh, wa-eh...' — the first day anyone was to hear his voice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 28, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: He went on till he caught Anansi, and when he saw him he told the little puppy to catch him — but the puppy, remembering, threw the bush on the fallen. The witch poked the bow through Anansi's two ears, built up a fire, and burned Anansi to dust — the teller ended with the customary 'Jack man dora!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 28, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Cowitch Tree and Mr. Foolman

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 29 'The Cowitch and Mr. Foolman' (told by Moses Hendricks, Mandeville)

summary.en: A gentleman offers the pick of his best cow to whoever fells the stinging cowitch tree without scratching — a test many have failed. Anansi takes the challenge and, as the poisonous juice burns him, narrates an imaginary piebald cow ('white here, black here, had a red here...') while scratching himself with each clause until the tree is down. To move the prize he hires Foolman, the fool who is not one: sent off for fire, Foolman butchers the cow, plants the tail like a stake, and hollers that the beast has escaped — the tail snaps in the tug-of-war, and Anansi keeps only the stub.
summary.zh: 紳士懸賞：砍倒毒漆樹而不撓癢者可得最好的牛。許多人皆敗；蜘蛛人應徵，樹汁灼膚之際，他口述想像中的花牛『此處白、此處黑、此處紅……』每說一處便撓一處，砍倒了大樹。運牛時他雇了『愚人先生』——愚人不愚：支去取火，愚人一家就地宰牛，把牛尾栽土作樁，高喊牛已逃走。拔河般的拉扯中牛尾斷裂，蜘蛛人只得分得一截尾梢。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; 'Foolman' trickster-reversal type. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: A gentleman had a cowitch property — a tree whose juice burns — and wanted it cut down; whoever cut it must not scratch his skin, and the reward was the pick of the best cow on the property. Many tried and failed. Anansi said he would cut it down, and the gentleman sent his son to watch. Anansi began cutting and the juice began to eat him; wanting to scratch, he told the boy, 'Young massa, the cow your papa is going to give me — white here (scratching one side), black here (scratching the other), had a red here, and another black here, blue just down at his feet' — and went on that way until he cut down the tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 29 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: He won the cow but could not move it alone and did not want an intelligent helper — he wanted a fool; so he hired a man called Foolman, who was not such a fool as he thought. They moved the cow to a butchering place near Foolman's yard, which Anansi did not know. Anansi sent Foolman off for fire toward a little smoke a long way off; no sooner was he gone than Foolman called up his family, butchered the cow, removed all the parts, leaving the tail — dug a hole and drove the root of the tail down tight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 29, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: When it was time for Anansi to return, Foolman held the tail-hair and called out, 'Brer Nansi, run! Brer Nansi, run!' Anansi came; Foolman said the whole cow was gone — only the tail — and both thought to pull the cow up out of the ground. While pulling, the tail broke in two, and Anansi had to give Foolman the piece that popped off. With all his cunning, he got but a very small piece.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 29, ending (1924); not verbatim.

region.zh: 牙買加曼德維爾與和諧堂

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 30 'Dry-Head and Anansi' (a, George Parkes; b, Ezekiel Williams)

summary.en: To eat a valued pig alone, Anansi feigns death-sickness, overtakes his wife on the road disguised as a doctor, and prescribes: kill the hog and let the patient eat it. Roasting the pig alone in the bush, he is muscled out of his own meat by the big-bellied bully Go-long-go — and gets revenge by luring the glutton into a ring of plant-trash soaked in oil. In the paired tale Anansi digs up Dry-head dropped from a tree — 'if you take me up, you take up trouble; if you put me down, you put down your luck' — cooks a fat barrow with him, and eats the whole pot clean because Dry-head has no hands to hold a spoon.
summary.zh: 為獨吞豬隻，蜘蛛人裝病垂死，又扮醫生在路上迎住妻子，開方：殺豬、病人獨食。林中獨自烤豬時，大肚惡霸戈隆戈強奪其肉；蜘蛛人以浸油的枯柴圈困饕餮報仇。另一篇：蜘蛛人掘起自樹上墜落的乾頭——『拾我即拾禍，棄我即棄運』——與之同煮肥豬；趁乾頭無手持匙，把整鍋肉吃個精光。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tales; 'Dry-head' is a spider-spirit of the sea in Jamaican tellings. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi's wife had a very large pig, valued at ten pounds, meant for the land it would buy. Anansi wanted to eat it — alone — so he fawned sick, very very sick, refusing everything. The wife dressed to go to the doctor; Anansi slipped out the other way, changed himself into a different man, and met her on the road. 'My husband is sick unto death!' 'I am the doctor. Have you any hog at home? If you want your husband to live, kill the hog and let him alone eat it.' The woman turned back with a heavy heart; Anansi ran home by the short cut and was in bed when she returned with the doctor's order. 'Cho! Doctor talking nonsense! How he think I eat such a big hog like that?' — 'To get you better, I got to comply with the doctor's order.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 30a 'Go-long-go' (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Anansi carried the hog into a wood alone, scraped and boiled it; digging a wild yam to cook with the meat, he was found by Brar Go-long-go, who demanded meat and threatened to stop his mouth and breath. Anansi took out piece after piece, then the whole of it, set it before Go-long-go — who ate off the whole of it. Anansi led him to a stretch of guinea-pea, put him in the middle of the plant-trash with a pint of oil thrown round about, and lit it. 'Come take me out!' cried Go-long-go from the fire. 'Nyam meat no gimme me no!' said Anansi — you ate the meat and gave me none.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 30a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the paired tale Anansi, traveling and fond of duckano, heard something drop 'ivoof' — and it was Brar Dry-head fallen off a tree. 'If you take me up, you take up trouble; and if you put me down, you put down your luck,' said Dry-head. Anansi, not knowing what to do, took him up: they killed a big fat barrow and boiled the pot. 'Brar Dry-head, you know what we do? Whoever cannot eat without a spoon must not taste it' — and Dry-head, who never had any hands, watched Anansi eat the pot off clean.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 30b 'Dry-head' (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Yam-hills and the Counting Taboo

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 31 'The Yam-hills' (told by George Parkes, Mandeville)

summary.en: Anansi digs nine yam-hills by the roadside under a taboo: whoever counts up to the number nine drops dead. He sets a weeping trap by his field; Hog counts to nine and falls; Goat shares the fate; day after day Anansi digs the same hills and eats the counters. But Monkey watches from a tree, comes down, counts 'one, two, three... eight, and the one Br'er Anansi sits down upon' — and the spider, stung by the cheat, snaps out the forbidden nine himself and drops dead. 'You can fool the others, but you can't fool me.'
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人在路邊掘九座薯壟，立禁：數至『九』者立死。他在田頭設哭局；豬數到九倒地，山羊同命；日復一日，蜘蛛人重掘薯壟，飽食數數者。猴兒樹上窺視多時，下樹數道：『一、二、三……八，再加上蜘蛛人坐著的那一座』——蜘蛛人被激，親口吐出犯禁的『九』字，應聲倒斃。『你能騙別人，騙不了我。』

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale built on a counting taboo; the taboo structure links to Yoruba hidden-name traditions (cross-ref motif family).

passages.text: Anansi worked a ground at the road-side, cleared his field, and dug nine yam-hills. Now no one was allowed to count up to the nine: whoever said 'nine' dropped down dead. Anansi sat down and began to cry. Hog passing asked what was the matter. 'My dear Bredder Hog, from mawning I dig these few yam-hills and try to count them, but I can't manage to count them yet.' — 'Cho! you too worthless! You mean say you can't say One, two, free, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine?' And as Hog said 'nine', Hog dropped down dead. Anansi took him up, put him in his bag, carried him home and ate him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 31 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The next day he came back and ate up Goat, who shared the same fate as Hog; every day he went back and dug the same hills. Monkey was on a tree watching all that took place. He came down, and while Anansi dug the nine hills again and sat crying, Monkey said, 'I will count them for you, but you must sit down upon one.' Then: 'One, two, free, four, five, six, seven, eight — and the one Br'er Anansi sit down upon.' Anansi, a man with a very short heart, got vex: 'You mean to say you can't say One, two, free, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine?' And as the word nine came out, Anansi dropped down dead. Monkey took him up and said, 'You can fool the others, but you can't fool me!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 31, ending (1924); not verbatim.

region.zh: 牙買加曼德維爾與和諧堂

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 32 'The Law Against Back-biting' (a, George Parkes; b, Alexander Archibald)

summary.en: In a hard-country law, whoever speaks ill of another drops dead. Anansi makes himself the bait: knocking stones on a roadside rock as if ploughing, he draws Hog, Cow, Horse and Goat into murmuring 'other men work good ground; Anansi works on rock' — each dies and is bagged. But Duck only dreams aloud of going to marry at the bottom yonder, and Anansi, tattling on him, drops dead himself; Duck swallows him — 'that's the way you talk a man!' In the paired version the disguised Guinea-chick passes in silence and the spider, calling him fool, dies for it.
summary.zh: 苦旱之邦立法：背誹他人者立死。蜘蛛人自為餌：在路邊岩石上敲鋤作耕地狀，誘豬、牛、馬、羊相繼嘀咕『別人耕好地，蜘蛛人卻耕石頭』——一個個倒斃入袋。鴨子卻只夢見去下游擇偶；蜘蛛人背地譏誚，自己應法而死，鴨子把他吞下——『這就是你們議論人的下場！』另一版本：喬裝的幾內亞雞默然走過，蜘蛛人罵聲『蠢貨』，當場斃命。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; taboo-of-speech structure shared with West African origin tales (cross-ref motif family).

passages.text: One time the country was very hard, and they passed a law that anyone who talked one another would drop down dead. Anansi said he must eat something out of it: he got a hoe, a pick-axe and a machete and went to a broad flat rock near the roadside where everyone passed, and began to knock — pong, pong, pong. Hog asked what he did there; Anansi said the governor had passed a law that famine was coming upon the land and everybody must work ground. Hog went on a little way and murmured, 'Odder people work ground a good place; Anansi deh work ground 'pon rock!' — and as Hog said so, he dropped down dead. Anansi picked him up, put him in his bag — 'Dat de way oonoo talk a man!' — carried Hog home and ate him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 32a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The next day Cow passed and shared Hog's fate; Horse and Goat came and shared it too. Then Duck came up and, asked for the strange news of his side, said only that he had dreamed a dream last night — that he had been on the world so long and never married yet, so he was going down to the bottom yonder to see if he could get married. When he went on, Anansi said, 'Good people they get married — Duck and all say him want to married too!' — and Anansi dropped down dead. Duck turned round, picked him up, swallowed him, and said, 'Dat's the way oonoo talk a man!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 32a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the paired version Guinea-chick dressed his clothes as if going to market, tied his head with a check handkerchief, passed Anansi digging on the rock-stone, and spoke no word at all. When he was gone past, Anansi said, 'Dat dar fool!' — and Anansi dropped dead. Jack man dora!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 32b 'Guinea-chick' (1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 33 'Fling-a-mile' (told by George Parkes, Mandeville)

summary.en: Something in a riverside hole grips Anansi's hand, names itself Fling-a-mile, and hurls him a mile. Back he comes with six iron and six wooden forks planted where he fell. Then, day by day, he escorts Hog, Goat and Dog to fish on the fatal side of the stream, admiring the pretty hole before each in turn, coaching each through the fatal formula — 'Fling me a mile mak I see' — until the flung bodies land on the stakes and the bag fills. But Monkey has watched from the tree, refuses the trick, pushes Anansi's own hand into the hole, and runs only halfway to pull the stakes out too late: Anansi lands on the forks, belly burst stiff dead.
summary.zh: 河邊洞中之物攥住蜘蛛人的手，自名『擲出一哩』，把他拋出一哩之遙。他回來在落點插下六支鐵叉六支木叉。此後日復一日，他陪豬、羊、狗到洞口一側釣魚，連聲讚歎『好一個漂亮的洞』，誘其伸手、教其念出致命口訣『擲我一哩讓我看看』——拋落的屍身正中叉陣，袋子裝滿。猴子樹上看得明白，拒不受騙，反把蜘蛛人的手按入洞中，又只跑半程去拔叉——蜘蛛人擲落叉尖，肚裂而死。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; answer-back ogre type (cf. ATU formula tales). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi went to the river to catch fish and came across a hole. He put his hand down in the hole and something held it. 'A who hold me?' — 'No me.' — 'Me who?' — 'No me, Fling-a-mile!' Anansi said, 'Fling me a mile mak I see.' The thing wheeled Anansi, wheeled him, and flung him one mile from the spot; when he dropped he nearly knocked out his senses. 'I must eat something out of that hole!' He got six iron forks and six wooden ones and stuck them up at the place where he dropped.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 33 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next day he met Hog going to fish. Anansi walked on the safe side, Hog on the side of the hole; 'What a pretty hole in front of Bredder Hog deh! You must get something out of it. Put your hand in, see if you feel anything.' Something held Hog's hand; Anansi coached the questions — A who hold me? — No me — Me who? — No me Fling-a-mile — 'Tell him fling you a mile mak you see!' The thing wheeled Hog, wheeled him, wheeled him, and dropped him right on the forks Anansi fixed up. Hog dropped dead; Anansi put him in his bag. Goat and Dog followed the same road the next two days, and Monkey watched from a tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 33, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Monkey could bear it no longer and put himself in Anansi's way. At the river, Monkey walked on the side where the hole was and Anansi on the opposite; 'What a pretty hole in front of Br'er Monkey! Put your hand in deh' — but Monkey refused: 'You come put your hand in deah.' As Anansi made the attempt, Monkey pushed his hand down, and the something held Anansi's hand now. Through the feeble formula — A me Fling-a-mile — 'Fling me a mile mak I see!' While it wheeled him, Anansi shouted to Monkey to run one mile and pull out the iron and wooden forks; Monkey took off his hat, ran half way, and stopped where he could watch. Anansi dropped on the forks and his belly burst, stiff dead — and Monkey took him, put him in his bag, and went to eat him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 33, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: But-but and Anansi: the Dresser in the Road
title.zh: 布特布特與蜘蛛人：路上的變換者

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 34 'But-but and Anansi' (told by Richard Morgan, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Anansi eats half his friend But-but's pone on the road to town, then buys everything in town. But-but lays wait, transforms into a red pocket-handkerchief, then a silver cup, then old drawers by the horse-pond — and each treasure Anansi admires and tosses aside for suspicion, until the 'old drawers' go into his own food-basket, and But-but eats the purchases off his head. Landing on the heads of Anansi's family, the bird lets the spider club each 'sleeping' child and then his wife dead, then perches on Anansi's own skull so the ridge-pole fall breaks the spider's neck.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人在往鎮的路上吃掉朋友布特布特一半的玉米糕，到鎮上買空一切。布特布特沿途設伏，先化紅手帕，再化銀盃，再化作馬塘邊的舊襯褲——蜘蛛人每得『寶物』皆疑而棄之，直到『舊襯褲』落進他自己的食籃，布特布特便在籃中吃光一切。隨後落在蜘蛛人家人的頭頂，蜘蛛人揮杵逐一『打死睡著的孩子』，連妻亦斃；布特布特最後停在蜘蛛人自己的頭上，蜘蛛人倒掛屋脊欲擊，跌落折頸而亡。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; the 'old drawers' taboo (never leave a worn garment about, lest a sorcerer use it) is explained in Beckwith's note and is reflected here.

passages.text: But-but and Anansi were going up to town. At the pass Anansi said, 'Brar But-but, let we eat your pone!' and they ate half of it; when But-but felt hungry later, Anansi said, 'You too foolish! we no half get to town yet.' But-but walked till he fainted away; Anansi traveled round a turn, stopped, and ate off his own pone there. In town Anansi bought everything in the whole town, loading a big cutacoo basket.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 34 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: But-but lay in wait part of the way home, flying on before and turning himself into a red pocket-handkerchief. Anansi came down and took it up — 'Yah! there's a good red pocket-handkerchief, but Brar But-but so cunnie, maybe he turn it!' — and flung it down. A little further, But-but turned a nice silver cup; Anansi admired his luck and threw it down too. At the horse-pond where his wife was washing, But-but turned a pair of old drawers; Anansi, blaming himself for carelessness, threw the 'old drawers' into his own cutacoo, and But-but began and ate out everything upon the basket-head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 34, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Anansi opened his basket at home, But-but flew out onto the first child's head. Anansi said, 'Stand steady, me baby, make I kill him!' and with a mortar-stick killed the child — 'dat no deady, on'y sleeping!' — then the second, then the third, then his wife ('you is the stronger head now!'). But-but flew onto Anansi's own head; the spider went up on the ridge-pole of the house and turned head-downward to strike the bird on his skull, fell halfway and caught, But-but flew off — and Anansi broke his neck. So But-but destroyed the whole family.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 34, ending (1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 35 'Tumble-bug and Anansi' (told by Moses Hendricks, Mandeville)

summary.en: Paid together for a job, Anansi buys plantains and a keg of butter and boxes his partner for dipping without 'permission' — Tumble-bug fawns dead, and the spider, certain he has killed him, flees to the woods leaving the whole feast. Tumble-bug wakes, eats everything, flies after him, and hides against a tree sounding like a man cutting bread-nut: 'Anansi kill Tumble-bug — life for life!' The spider runs to 'Dead man country', gets among the dry trash, and lives there ever since.
summary.zh: 二人同做一份工得錢，蜘蛛人買了大蕉與一桶牛油，因推糞蟲『未經許可』蘸醬而一拳打去；推糞蟲裝死，蜘蛛人以為殺了人，棄下盛宴逃入林中。推糞蟲醒來吃盡一切，隨後追蹤而至，倚樹藏身，學人砍面包果之聲：『蜘蛛人殺了推糞蟲——以命償命！』蜘蛛人逃進『死人國』，鑽入碎柴堆中，自此便住在那裡。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale with etiological ending (beetle lives in dung/trash). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi and Tumble-bug took a job together. After they got their pay, Anansi said they must buy something for a good feed, and they bought a bunch of plantains and a keg of butter. They commenced to eat — Anansi dip, Tumble-bug dip. 'No, my Tumble-bug, when I go kpluck-um, you must go tip!' Tumble-bug dipped all the same; Anansi got vex and boxed him. Tumble-bug fawned dead. Anansi, frightened — 'Hi! Tumble-bug, the least bit of fun I make with you, you dead?' — ran off leaving butter, plantains and everything, and took to the woods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 35 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tumble-bug woke up, ate up the plantains and the butter, and flew after Anansi. In the woods near where Anansi hid, he placed himself against a tree and gave a sound like a man cutting. 'Who are you?' called Anansi. 'Gentleman servant cutting bread-nut for gentleman horse.' — 'Hear any news?' — 'Yes.' — 'What you hear?' — 'Anansi kill Tumble-bug — life for life!' Anansi started running and Tumble-bug after him; he ran out to a place called Dead man country, got among the dry trash, and that is where he has lived ever since.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 35, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Horse Sent for Fire, Goat Waits Behind the Bush

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 36 'Horse and Anansi' (told by Alexander Archibald, Mandeville)

summary.en: After cutting plantains, Anansi sends galloping Horse off for fire at 'quite yonder' — and roasts and eats everything with his own tinder-box, blaming a passing man for stealing the roast. Horse gets two plantains; Goat, who has watched from the bush, insists on going with Anansi next day, trots off for the fire and doubles back to spy — then circles the roasting fire with a cut stick, driving the spider hand by hand into the ring, and carries away everything, not giving Anansi one.
summary.zh: 砍完大蕉，蜘蛛人遣馬奔向『遠處』取火——自己用火絨盒生火烤食一切，僅留四根，還誣稱有路人搶走。馬只得兩根；山羊在灌木後看得明白，次日執意同去，領命取火後繞叢折返窺視——隨後手持砍刀繞火成圈，把蜘蛛人的手一步步圈進來，盡取其食，一根不留。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; the fire-errand ruse is a widespread African-diaspora motif (cf. fire-theft cluster).

passages.text: Anansi called Horse to go into the bush and cut plantains. When they had cut them and carried them out into the open and begun to play at lick-stick, Anansi said, 'Brar Horse, we hungry now, and we have no fire to roast the plantains. See fire quite yonder? Go take fire, come, make we roast plantain!' Horse flung up his tail and galloped off. Meanwhile Anansi struck his tinder-box, built a fire, roasted every plantain, ate them all, and left only four.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 36 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Horse galloped and could not catch the fire and turned back. Anansi said, 'Brar Horse, when you were gone, one man passed here and gave me fire and I roasted the plantains; as soon as my roasting was done, one man came and beat me and took away the plantains, only leaving these four for me!' — 'Never mind! you take two, me take two.' So Horse took two. That time Brar Goat went into the bush and knelt down watching what took place; so the next day Goat said he would go with Anansi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 36, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The two went, cut plantains, came out into the open and played. 'Brar Goat, we hungry now and we have no fire. See fire quite yonder? gallop and get fire and come.' Goat galloped, went round a clump of bush, knelt down on his knee and watched. Anansi struck his tinder-box, made a fire, peeled every plantain and put them on; when they roasted he scraped every bit. As he scraped, Goat got up and came; Goat cut a stick, jumped one side so as to put a circle round the fire-side, and said to Anansi, 'Put your hand in now, sah!' — jumped the other side and put the circle again. Anansi began to beg, and Goat took away everything, didn't give him one. Jack man dora!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 36, ending (1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 37a 'Bunya' (told by Elizabeth Hilton, Harmony Hall)

summary.en: Anansi puts on a big pot of water and teaches Monkey country the password: when I say 'Bunya', take me out. In he goes, cries Bunya at the first scald, comes out steaming — and the monkeys all climb in. Every 'Bunya!' from the pot is answered 'No bunya yet!' until they boil, and Anansi eats them. One little monkey escapes scalded from the pot-rim, carries the story to the next Monkey country, and there, when Anansi tries his password again, the monkeys hold him in the pot till he is killed.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人架起大水鍋，教猴國暗號：我喊『布尼亞』便放我出鍋。他一入鍋，水一燙便喊，蒸騰而出；猴群爭相入鍋。鍋中聲聲『布尼亞！』，鍋外聲聲『還沒到布尼亞！』直至煮爛，蜘蛛人大快朵頤。一隻小猴從鍋沿逃出生天，報信於鄰國猴群；蜘蛛人再施故技時，眾猴扣他入鍋，直到把他煮死。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale (password reversal type). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi went to Monkey country and put on a big pot of water. He told the monkeys: when I get in the pot of water and say 'Bunya', you must take me out — then you may go in. When he went into the pot, as soon as he felt the water hot he said 'Bunya,' and they took him out; then they put all of them into the pot of water at one time. When they said 'Bunya!' Anansi said, 'No bunya yet!' — again and again — and would not take them out until they boiled. Anansi took them out and ate them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 37a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: One little one was left at the top of the pot where the water did not scald. That one ran to the next Monkey country and told them the story of Anansi and the 'bunya'. When Anansi had eaten, he started for the other country, went there, and told the monkeys to put him into the pot of water and take him out when he said 'Bunya'. When Anansi felt the water hot, he said 'Bunya!' The monkeys said, 'No bunya yet!' — and kept Anansi in that pot until they killed him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 37a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Anansi in Monkey Country: Christen Christen
title.zh: 蜘蛛人闖猴國：受洗受洗

region.zh: 牙買加聖安克萊爾蒙特

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 37b 'Christen Christen' (told by Adolphus Iron, Claremont)

summary.en: In famine, Anansi travels to Monkey country to preach a christening 'with a large oven'. The monkeys build and fire it; Anansi goes in first and cries 'Chris'en!' — they open the door, he leaps out, and the monkeys leap in; when the last is in, Anansi shuts the door. Their cries of 'Chris'en! chris'en!' are answered 'No chris'en yet!' until one scorched-sided survivor escapes to warn the next country — where the rebuilt oven is fired hotter, and the password is held until Anansi bursts.
summary.zh: 饑年之中，蜘蛛人赴猴國『佈道受洗』，聲稱要用大烤爐。猴群欣然築爐生火；蜘蛛人先入，喊『受洗！』——爐門開，他跳出，猴群爭相跳入；最後一隻入爐，蜘蛛人關門。爐中『受洗！受洗！』之呼，換來聲聲『還沒受洗！』直到一隻燒焦半身的倖存者逃往鄰國報信。蜘蛛人再到時，猴群把爐燒得更旺，扣住暗號不放，直烤到他肚裂而亡。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; 'christen' frame is folk-comic use of a church term, not religious instruction material. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: One time hard time caught Brar Nansi; he could get nothing to eat, and traveled away to Monkey country to go preach. When he got there he said, 'Well, friends, I come here to chris'en, but I chris'en wid a large oven.' The monkeys were glad to hear it; they jumped and built up the oven. Anansi said, 'You must pack it with wood and light it with fire. When it is well hot, I will go in first, and when you hear me say Chris'en, you must open the door.' The monkeys agreed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 37b (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The oven built, the oven lit, Anansi went in. He hollered 'Chris'en!' — they opened the door, Anansi jumped out, and the monkeys began to jump in. When the last monkey jumped in, Anansi shut the door. The monkeys began to holler 'Chris'en! chris'en!' — Anansi said, 'No chris'en yet!' When he thought they were well roasted, he opened the door; one scorched-sided one jumped out and ran to the other Monkey country to tell all that was done. Anansi stood there till he had eaten off the whole of the roasted ones.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 37b, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: He traveled again till he caught the other Monkey country, all prepared to meet him; the scorched-sided one met him first. 'Brar, I think I know you!' — 'No, sah, it is the first time I and you buck up!' Anansi proposed his christening with the oven; the monkeys built it up quicker yet. 'I will go in first; when you hear me say Chris'n, you open the door.' When Anansi felt the fire he hollered, 'Chris'n, chris'n, chris'n!' — and the monkeys said, 'No chris'n yet!' — and let Anansi stay all roasted till he burst.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 37b, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Curing the Sick: the Six Children

texts.period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924 note (published 1924)

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 38b 'The Six Children' (told by George Parkes, Mandeville)

summary.en: An old woman's six children weep by the roadside over her blindness; Hog, Goat, Cow and Jack-ass pass and confess they cannot cure. Anansi stops, promises the cure, and orders a feast laid in the kitchen — barrel of water, two barrels of yam, butter, lard, plenty meat. He shuts himself in with the mother and, when all is cooked and fried, cries 'fee-e-e-e'; outside, the children sing 'Tank God, mama have a cure!' — while Anansi eats everything, stacks the bones at the fire-side, and fastens the door for nine days. On the seventh the children burst in and find their mother's bones; Jack-ass, the only helper to return, fawns dead with a swollen belly, takes in the spider's arm to the shoulder, and gallops him to the children's yard to be burnt until his belly bursts.
summary.zh: 老婦六子臨路而泣，為母之目盲；豬、羊、牛、驢相繼而過皆稱無能為力。蜘蛛人應下治病之諾，令備盛宴於廚——一桶水、兩桶白薯、牛油、豬油與足量肉。他閉門與老婦獨處，烹煮煎炸既畢，喊一聲『咿——』；門外孩子們唱道『謝天謝地，媽媽有救了！』——蜘蛛人卻吃盡一切，把骨頭堆在爐邊，鎖門九日。第七日孩子破門而入，只見母親骸骨。驢是唯一回來的幫手，詐死鼓腹，任蜘蛛人的手臂沒至肩膀，直奔孩子家院，把蜘蛛人丟進大火燒到肚裂。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale (fake-healer swindle type); dark comedy from named tellers.

passages.text: An old woman had six children, three sons and three daughters, living near the roadside. The old woman was sick with sore eyes, so the children came out by the wayside and began to cry. Hog passing asked what was the matter — 'Our mother became blind and we cannot cure it!' — 'I can't do no good!' Goat, Cow and Jack-ass passed in turn and each confessed the same. Then Anansi came up, heard the crying, and said, 'I can cure it! Put a barrel of water in the kitchen, two barrels of white yam, a pound of butter, a pound of lard, enough meat, and I'll come back another day and cure it!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 38b (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the appointed day he came back, had the mother carried into the kitchen, shut the door, and told the children: when you hear something say 'fee-e-e-e', you must all say, 'Tank God, mama have a cure!' Anansi killed the old lady, cooked off all the yams and flour and everything, fried up the old lady with the butter and the lard, went 'fee-e-e-e' — and the children hearing it sang 'Tank God, mama have a cure!' while Anansi ate off the old lady and all the things, packed the bones at the fire-side, fastened the door, and said they must not open it for nine days.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 38b, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the seventh day the children could bear it no longer, burst the door open, and found all their mother's bones at the fire-side. Out they came crying again; Jack-ass, the only one to promise help, went to Anansi's gate and lay down fawning dead with his belly swollen. Anansi came down — 'Lawd! that's a lot me bwoy meet up today!' — sent for the big pot and bowl and yabba and knife, cut the jackass under the belly, filled pot and bowl with fat, and shoved his arm clear to his shoulder for the yabba. Jack-ass held him. 'Fun or no fun, come we go!' — Jack-ass got up and galloped straight to the children's yard, and they made up a big fire and put Anansi in and burnt him and burnt him till his belly burst.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 38b, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Anansi, White-belly and Fish: why Fishes Are Eaten
title.zh: 蜘蛛人、白腹與魚：食魚之由

region.en: Maggotty, Jamaica (symbolic pin: Santa Cruz river country)
region.zh: 牙買加馬戈蒂（象徵定位：聖克魯斯河地）

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 39 'Anansi, White-belly and Fish' (told by Mrs. Ramialli, Maggotty)

summary.en: Fitted out with borrowed wings to join White-belly's feeding-trees over the river, Anansi claims every tree as his own, eats himself asleep — and the offended bird strips the false wings so the spider turns in his sleep and falls into the river. Rescued as 'cousin' by Fish, he out-fools the hot rice-pop test, poaches a whole barrel of eggs in the ashes and carries them off one marked egg at a time — until Fish's shout across the water is misheard by her own children, who row the 'stranger man' safely home in the bag. And from that day, fishes are eaten.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人借得雙翅隨白腹上樹覓食，卻逢樹便稱『這是我的樹』，吃到酣睡；白腹負氣拆其假翅，蜘蛛人翻身墜河。魚以『表兄』相救，他反把熱粥考驗倒轉來騙；又在灰中焐熟整整一桶魚蛋，凭一枚反覆標記的蛋偷走全部。渡河時魚母隔水喊話被孩子們誤聽成『快划』，蜘蛛人把兩條小魚裝袋帶回家吃掉——從那天起，魚便被人吃了。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale with etiological ending (why fish are eaten). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi lay in the sun every morning watching the birds go to feed. One day he said to White-belly, 'Brar White-belly, where you go to feed every day? Take me with you.' White-belly promised on condition that he would behave himself, fitted him out with a pair of wings to fly, and they went to the feeding-trees, which overhung a river. Every tree White-belly went on, Anansi said, 'A fe me tree dat!' and White-belly went away to another. Anansi ate so much that he fell fast asleep; White-belly got annoyed, went and took off the false wings, and Anansi turned in his sleep and fell into the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 39 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Fish picked him up and took him to their home. 'Cousin Fish, no eat me!' — 'If we are cousin, we wi' see!' Fish boiled hot rice-pop; Anansi said it was not hot enough — put it in the sun to make it hotter — then drank it off to the last. That night he begged a bed in the kitchen where Fish kept a barrel of eggs, poached all the eggs in the ashes, left one, and marked it; each time the mother Fish counted, he wiped the mark off and brought back the same egg, until he had taken the whole barrel full.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 39, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: When he wanted to go, Fish told two of the children to get the canoe and take their cousin over the river. Halfway across, Fish bawled out at the top of her voice, 'Bring stranger man back he-e-ah! for he eat off all me eggs; only one is here!' — but Anansi told the children their mother said to row quickly and squall ahead, and they rowed across. Anansi took them up, put them in his bag, took them home and ate them. And from that day, fishes are eaten.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 39, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Goat's Escape: the Rain and the Dance

region.en: Claremont, St. Ann, and Maroon Town, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖安克萊爾蒙特與馬倫鎮

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 40 'Goat's Escape' (a, Richard Pottinger; b, Elizabeth Hilton and Alfred Williams)

summary.en: Goat, afraid of rain, is forced by a drizzle into Anansi's house, where the fiddler sings his thanks to Brar Rain for driving wild meat in from the bush — and Goat bolts through the door, cannot cross the river, turns himself into a little white stone, and is thrown over the water by Dog's ruse to land on four feet on the far bank: 'Luck in me hand and it get away!' In the dance version, Anansi stations himself at one door to close it while Goat and Dog escape through the other; Dog swims, Goat turns to a rock by the roadside, and Anansi's thrown boulder answers 'Baa-a-a-a!' — for which Assono, so vexed, eats Anansi up in the same place.
summary.zh: 山羊怕雨，被細雨逼入蜘蛛人家；蜘蛛人拉琴唱『謝雨神自林中趕來野肉』——山羊奪門而出，無法渡河，化為溪畔小白石；狗設計讓蜘蛛人把石頭拋過河，山羊四腳著地落在對岸：『運氣在我手卻溜走了！』舞會篇：蜘蛛人守一門欲關之，山羊與狗自另一門逃脫；狗會游泳，山羊化作路旁巨岩；蜘蛛人擲石過河，岩上應聲『咩——』，阿索諾大怒，就地把蜘蛛人吃了。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale with transformation motifs. 'Assono' is an unidentified large animal in Beckwith's cycle.

passages.text: Anansi and Goat had a little quarrel. Anansi said, 'Brar Goat, I gwine catch you!' Goat said, 'You never live, me friend, to catch me!' Goat was afraid of rain; so one moist night, coming from his field, he had to pass Anansi's house as drizzle-drizzle rain fell, and ran up. 'Come in, me friend!' Goat went in. Anansi stepped into a room, took out his fiddle, and sang: 'Me thank Brar Rain, fe run wil' meat from bush, come a house.' Goat kept to the doorway; Anansi, playing the same song, did not notice as Goat jumped down the bottom of the door — and cut after him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 40a 'The Rain' (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Goat could not cross the river, ran to the river-side and turned into a white little stone. Dog, on the other side, saw when Goat turned into the little stone. Anansi ran up the river: 'Brar Dog, see Brar Goat pass?' — 'Yes, Brar! see one little stone a river-side deh? Take it up, throw it over, I show you where he is.' Anansi took up the stone and threw it to the other side to Brar Dog — and Goat dropped on his four feet. Anansi said, 'Luck in me hand and it get away!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 40a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the dance version, Anansi made a bargain with Assono that when Goat and Dog came in to the dance, Assono would sit at one door and Anansi at the other. When Anansi proposed taking the fiddle to play on the doormat for the two slow singers, that was the moment he meant to shut the door — but Dog and Goat ran through the other door before Assono could catch them, Anansi and Assono chased them to a big river; Dog swam over and left Goat, who turned into a big rock and lay by the roadside. Dog said to Anansi, 'Take a rock-stone, lick me down, and I will stay for you to come pick me up!' Anansi flung a big rock over the river — and Goat got up and hollered 'Baa-a-a-a!' Assono was so vexed with Anansi that he ate him up in the same place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 40b 'The Dance' (1924); not verbatim.
